comment.value: The paper introduces the Graph invAriant Learning Assistant (GALA), a novel framework for learning invariant graph representations. The paper proves the limitation of existing environment augmentation, and establish minimal assumptions—variation sufficiency and variation consistency—for invariant graph learning. They introduce an assistant model to distinguish variations in spurious subgraphs, thereby enhancing robustness against environmental shifts.  Empirical results, both synthetic and real-world, convincingly validate the efficacy of GALA. The paper is well-structured, clear, and supported by comprehensive experiments and theoretical analyses. Overall, this work advances the understanding of OOD in graph neural networks and should be accepted.

I thank the reviewer for their time and effort in making the rebuttal.
The authors have successfully addressed some of my concerns/questions, in particular regarding the position of this paper in the current state of the art.
However, having also read other reviews I was influenced by some of their points, like the concerns regarding the generalization capabilities of the method.
All things considered, I maintain my original score.

Thank you for checking our rebuttal and for your further comments. 

> Regarding the environment assistant model's ability to distinguish different environments

In fact, the current design of the environment assistant model aims to distinguish the variations of spurious features instead of the specific environment partitions. As spurious correlations are more unstable than invariant correlations (Variation sufficiency assumption), the partitioned positive and negative graph sets could amplify the instability of spurious correlations. Then, GALA could locate the invariant subgraphs by finding the subgraphs that preserve the maximal invariance across the positive and negative graph sets. As shown in Fig. 3a, no matter which of the invariant or spurious correlations is stronger (Variation consistency assumption), the invariant subgraph maintains the maximally invariant correlations across the positive and negative graph sets partitioned by a simple ERM-based model. 

Nevertheless, we agree there are limitations in the current design of the environment assistant model as you pointed out. Incorporating additional design such as selecting/identifying spurious features, or an even more biased assistant model, is definitely a promising future direction to extend and improve our framework. We have included the discussion in our revised draft.

Thank you again for your constructive comments and suggestions!

Thank you for your time in reviewing our work. Please see our detailed responses to your comments and suggestions below where we use reference numbers in our manuscript due to the character limit.

> W1 Problem definition

We complemented the problem definition in Sec. 2:

The goal of OOD generalization on graphs is to find a GNN $f$ that minimizes the maximal loss among all environments, i.e., to minimize $\max_{e\in \mathcal{E}_\text{all}} R^e$, where $R^e$ is the risk of $f$ under environment $e$.

> W2 Motivation of ``two-piece’’ graphs.

We have revised our paper to include the explanation for why adopting the two-piece graphs. The main reason is that the two-piece graph is the **minimal implementation** of PIIF distribution shifts in Fig. 2, which is more suitable for theoretical discussions. Specifically, PIIF distribution shifts in Fig. 2 model the invariant and spurious correlations via the correlation of subgraphs with the labels. For simplicity, we restrict the types of invariant and spurious subgraphs and use a simple flipping operation to simulate the invariant/spurious correlations, motivated by [25] that is used to discuss the failures of IRM[3].

> W3 Assumption 3.5

We have revised it following your suggestion.

> Q1 Understanding line 125.

By definition, the Rad function will flip the labels with a probability $\alpha$. Considering a $f^{G_c}_{gen}$ that maps +1 to a ``house`` subgraph and -1 to a ``cycle`` subgraph. Let the sampled $Y^e=+1$, and $\alpha=0.1$, then with a probability of 10%, $G_c$ will be a ``cycle`` and a probability of 90%, $G_c$ will be a ``house``.

> Q2 How GALA addresses the failure of environment generation?

In fact, the faithfulness of environment generation **relies on the success of partitioning the invariant and spurious subgraphs**, when without additional knowledge. If the model already learns to partition the graph, then it is unnecessary to generate any new environments. Otherwise, environment generation can hardly avoid generating harmful environments for OOD generalization on graphs, as shown in Proposition 3.2.

Therefore, **GALA avoids the failures of environment generation by not performing environment generation**. Instead, GALA aims to identify the maximal invariant subgraph among the partitioned subsets by the assistant model.

> Q3 Explanation of Proposition 3.4.

Any invariant graph learning algorithm accepts the input of the joint distribution $P(Y,G)$ and aims to identify an invariant subgraph $\widehat{G}_c$. Given the same $P(Y,G)$, the algorithm will stick to the same $\widehat{G}_c$:

If $\mathcal{E}\_\text{tr}$ and $\mathcal{E}\_\text{tr}’$ have the same $P(Y,G)$ but different underlying invariant subgraphs ($G_c$, $G_c’$ respectively, with $G_c\neq G_c’$). If the algorithm succeeds in one environment, for example, $\mathcal{E}\_{tr}$, and outputs $\widehat{G}\_c=G_c$ given the input $P(Y,G)$. Then, the algorithm will fail in $\mathcal{E}\_{tr}’$ as $\widehat{G}_c=G_c\neq G_c’$.

> Q4 Caption of Figure 1.

We need to clarify that **the black colored labels are the predictions yielded by the assistant model instead of the ground truth labels (in orange color)**. According to the correctness of the assistant model, we can partition the whole dataset into positive graphs (i.e., correctly predicted samples in the top left and the bottom right) and negative graphs (i.e., incorrectly predicted samples in the top right and the bottom left). GALA will pull graphs with the same ground truth label but from positive and negative graphs closer. 
We revised the caption to highlight that the labels are graph labels in the figure.

> Q5 The final loss.

Eq. 9 is implemented in a contrastive loss. We provide the specific loss in Eq. 18 of Appendix F. We revised the text around Eq. 9 to clarify this point.

Please let us know if you have any further questions. We’d be grateful if you could consider our responses above when making final evaluations of our work.

Thank you for taking the time in reviewing our work. Please see our detailed responses to your comments and suggestions below where we use reference numbers in our manuscript due to the character limit.

> W1 Notations

We understand it might be difficult for readers who are not familiar with the literature to follow our notations and hence provide a table of key notations in Appendix A for your reference.

We have revised our draft to include $e\in\mathcal{E}\_{all}$ in line 78. $\widehat{G}_c$ is the estimated subgraph, and we have added its definition before Eq 1, which is the output of the subgraph extractor. 

We also double checked and corrected the other parts of our draft.

> W2 Why focusing on graph data?

First, we need to clarify that, as pointed out in CIGA[6], OOD generalization on graphs is fundamentally more challenging than that in Euclidean data. Given that graph is a generalized form of Euclidean data (e.g., images, languages), **methods developed on graphs usually are not limited to graphs and can be applied directly to Euclidean data, but methods developed in Euclidean data can hardly be applied directly to graphs**.

The specialization of GALA for graph data mainly lies in three aspects:

- **The study of GALA is more desired by graph data**. Different from Euclidean data, all OOD methods on graph data [6,14,35,38,44,55,56,60,64] do not assume the availability of environment labels nor the auxiliary information [36]. Given the faithfulness of environment augmentation has never been discussed on graphs, the study of faithfulness is more desired by graph data.
- **Graph data is also a suitable testbed for GALA**. It can be found that, on the two-piece graph datasets that satisfy the theory well, GALA outperforms other methods by a large margin up to $30$% and $13%$% in average, owing to its theoretical guarantee.
- **GALA inherits the graph specific design from existing works** such as CIGA[6] and GSAT[44] that use information theory to handle the complexity of graph data and an interpretable GNN architecture to address graph distribution shifts modeled by the SCM in Fig. 2. Extracting the invariant subgraph is the central task specific for OOD generalization on graphs. Therefore, all of our theory and solution concentrates on the identifiability of the invariant subgraph.

> W3 Why ERM still learns spurious correlations in invariance-dominated cases?

It is theoretically proved in [8]. Intuitively, ERM will learn **any correlations presented in the data**, no matter whether the correlation is invariant or spurious. If we look into the first two columns in Table 1, it can be found that **GNNs trained with ERM still have a large gap from the oracle models**, meaning that GNNs trained with ERM still learn the spurious correlations. 

> Q1 Oracle performance

The Oracle performance is obtained via canceling the distribution shifts among training and test data by randomly re-splitting the whole dataset, following [6]. 

> Q2 Why DisC fails on all datasets except for CMNIST-sp and why only GALA and DisC succeed in CMNIST-sp?

CMNIST-sp is converted from the ColoredMNIST dataset[3] which contains severe spuriousness dominated shifts in node features. DisC is designed to tackle this kind of severe distribution shifts in CMNIST-sp via an **aggressive strategy** to discard the dominant patterns [14,46], and additionally incorporate environment generation procedure based on the aggressively separated subgraphs. However, the aggressive strategy in DisC may affect learning useful patterns for generalization and fails when the distribution shifts are mild. 

Other methods fail in CMNIST-sp because of various drawbacks. For example, GREA, CIGA can only handle invariance dominated cases. In contrast, GALA succeeds because of its theoretical guarantee in handling both invariance and spuriousness dominated cases.

> L1 Limitation discussion.

We actually provided the discussion of limitations and future works in Appendix B.

Please let us know if there are any further questions. We’d appreciate it if you could take the above responses into consideration when making the final evaluation of our work.

The SCM of Fig. 2 is primarily motivated by the real-world drug property prediction task[B], where the property of a drug molecule can usually be characterized by a sub-molecule or functional group (e.g., `-OH` to solubility). We have added the discussion to the introduction of Fig.2.

> W3 Listing contributions and comparing with [36]

We revised our paper and included a bullet list of our contributions:
- We identify failure cases of existing invariant graph learning approaches and establish the minimal assumptions for feasible invariant graph learning; 
- We develop a novel framework GALA with provable identifiability of the invariant subgraph for OOD generalization on graphs under the assumptions; 
- We conduct extensive experiments to verify both our theoretical results and the superiority of GALA;

Notably, both our theory and solution differ from Lin et al. [36] fundamentally in terms of **assumptions** and **methodology**. More specifically, we do not rely on the auxiliary information and are compatible with the existing interpretable and generalizable GNN architecture for OOD generalization on graphs.

> Q1 Connection with the explainability literature.

Thanks for pointing out the related work [A]. In fact, there is a deep connection between interpretability and generalizability [6,44]. As characterized by the SCMs (Fig. 2), only extracting and using the underlying invariant subgraph for the prediction can generalize under various graph distribution shifts (Proposition E.2 in [6]), meanwhile the extracted subgraph can also serve as the interpretable result for the prediction.

Both [A] and our work are inspired to incorporate causality in finding faithful interpretable subgraphs, while [A] focuses on *post-hoc explainability* given a trained GNN and ours focuses on *intrinsic interpretable GNN*. We have included the discussion of [A] in our revised draft.

We’d appreciate it if you could take the above responses into consideration when making the final evaluation of and supporting our work. Please let us know if there are any outstanding questions.

Thank you for your insightful comments and your support of our work! Please see our detailed responses to your comments and suggestions below where we use reference numbers in our manuscript due to the character limit.

> W1 How to guarantee the environment assistant model only learns environment dependent patterns? What about other biased ERM models?

We need to clarify that **we do not intend to let the environment assistant model learn only the environment dependent patterns**. Instead, the assistant model is also allowed to learn invariant patterns. Since spurious patterns are more likely to change between environments than invariant patterns (variation sufficiency), as shown in Fig. 3a, once the assistant model learns the spurious patterns, these spurious patterns can be differentiated from invariant ones across $\{G^p\}$ and $\{G^n\}$ according to the correctness of the predictions yielded by the assistant model. 

In experiments, we tried two types of ERM biased models: one is the vanilla GNN and the other is the interpretable GNN, where both of them bring improvements when incorporated into GALA. Besides, we also discussed more implementation choices in Appendix F. The results show that one could implement the assistant model to better fit the spurious patterns when additional knowledge is provided, which highlights a promising future direction as discussed in Appendix B.

> W2 What about training sets with equally correlated spurious and invariant patterns?

Although this case is gotten rid of by the variation consistency assumption for the impossibility of identifying an invariant subgraph, results in Fig. 5 show that GALA still brings certain improvements to previous methods. We hypothesize that there exist other factors, such as the size of spurious and invariant subgraphs, affect the fitting of spurious and invariant patterns, and consider discussing more factors other than correlation strength to the design of the assistant model as well as OOD generalization on graphs as a promising future direction.

> W3 Computational complexity of GALA.

Please let us know if you have any further questions. We’d be grateful if you could take the above responses into consideration when making the final evaluation of and supporting our work!

summary.value: Invariant graph learning methods aim to extract invariant patterns among different training environments for OOD generalization on graphs. A plethora of approaches focuses on augmenting environment information from training samples as the environment label is difficult to obtain. This work provides both theoretical and empirical analysis of the faithfulness of the existing environment augmentation methods for learning invariant graph representations. They demonstrate that it is impossible to learn invariant graph representations by environment augmentation without a set of minimal assumptions developed in the paper, including variation sufficiency and variation consistency. Based on these assumptions, they then propose GALA, Graph invAriant Learning Assistant, a new graph invariant learning framework via an assistant model providing proxy predictions to differentiate spurious variations. Experiments on 12 real-world graph OOD datasets demonstrate GALA's effectiveness.

strengths.value:
1. This paper is very well-written and organized. The problem studying (i.e., whether the existing environment augmentation methods are faithful for learning invariant graph representations) is significant, and the motivating synthetic experiments clearly demonstrate the pitfalls of existing environment augmentation.
2. Although the variation sufficiency and variation consistency assumptions seem intuitive, this paper is the first to develop these minimal assumptions systematically and utilize them to derive the impossibility results for existing methods.
3. GALA is technically sound and the authors provide theoretical analysis to demonstrate GALA is able to identify invariant subgraph patterns.
4. Experiments are comprehensive and extensive. The results of proof-of-concept and ablation studies are consistent with the theoretical results derived in the paper, and the real-world experiments demonstrate a considerable improvement among all the baselines.
5. The authors did a great job of citing related works (in the appendix).

weaknesses.value:
1. The environment assistant model is trained with vanilla ERM on spuriousness-dominated data to identify spurious correlations. My major concern is the vanilla ERM model should learn both spurious correlations and invariant patterns, and then how to guarantee the environment assistant model only learns environment-dependent patterns? I wonder if the authors have tried other biased ERM models as backbone and it would be great if they could elaborate more on this question.
2. In this paper, the authors divide the training sets into spuriousness-dominated and invariance-dominated sets. I wonder what if the whole training sets only contains spurious and invariance patterns distributed equally? 
3. The authors did not discuss the computational complexity of GALA. I wonder if they could discuss it in detail.

questions.value:
1. The 3 questions mentioned in the Weaknesses part.
2. Since this work is proposed to tackle OOD generalization on graphs, I wonder if the authors made some attempts on OOD generalization on Euclidean data?

limitations.value: The authors discussed the broader impacts in the appendix.

summary.value: This paper discusses the challenges of learning invariance among data from different environments for out-of-distribution generalization on graphs. The authors propose a new framework called Graph invAriant Learning Assistant (GALA) that incorporates an assistant model to differentiate the variations in spurious subgraphs. The paper also includes experiments on 12 datasets, including DrugOOD, with various graph distribution shifts to verify the superiority of GALA.

strengths.value:
- The paper tackles an interesting problem. Distributions shifts between training and test sets hinder and limit the potential applicability of graph neural networks methods into real world scenarios.
- To the best of my knowledge, the method proposed in this paper is novel.
- The paper is, mostly, well written and makes an effort to be easily understandable.
- The paper presents valid theoretical arguments to back its main claims.
- Finally, the paper presents an extensive sets of experiments that back the validity of the proposed method.

weaknesses.value:
- In the tables that contain results, the best values are bolded. However, the presentation of the results would be more fair if two different colours/markers would be used when the best result is within the confidence interval of another result.

- The paper would be easier to follow if, along figure 2, a plausible real world example was used.

- In the last part of the introduction section the authors convey their contributions. In my opinion, this part is one of the less clear in the paper. To improve the clarity, I suggest the authors make a bullet list of their contributions. In particular, I would like the authors to distinguish their original contributions and how they differ from the work of Lin et al [36].

questions.value:
I am interested in knowing if the authors believe there exists a connection between this work and the explainability literature. In particular, the counterfactual explainability subfield (like the work from [A], just to provide a reference).

_[A] Lucic, Ana, et al. "Cf-gnnexplainer: Counterfactual explanations for graph neural networks." International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics. PMLR, 2022._

summary.value: This paper investigates OOD problems on graphs without environmental information. The authors show that it is impossible to learn invariant graph representations without additional assumptions. The authors propose a novel graph OOD method namely GALA based on a new assumption. An auxiliary model is used to make proxy predictions and then the proxy predictions are used to help identify invariant subgraphs. Experiments on 12 datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed method.

strengths.value:
S1. The authors clearly demonstrate that the identifiability of causal subgraphs is ill-posed without environment labels. Thereby, the authors give A3.3 and A3.5 and then propose GALA based on these two assumptions.

S2. Both theoretical and experimental analyses are used to support the claim.

weaknesses.value:
W1. This is a math-heavy paper, but the notations are unclear to me, thus making it hard to read. For example, in lines 78-79, should there be something like $e \in \mathcal{E}_{all}$? In Equation 1, there is no definition about $\widehat{G}_c$. There are more examples, I will not list them all.

W2. I think GALA can be used as a general OOD method. Why do the authors focus on graph data? I don't see any specific design only for graphs. Why not test GALA on other data types (ex., images)?

W3. I don't understand why ERM still learns the spurious correlations in invariance dominated cases. Can this be justified theoretically?

questions.value:
Q1. I am confused about how to get the Oracle performance on these datasets. Can the authors provide more explanations?

Q2. I don't understand why Disc fails on all the datasets except CMNIST-sp. Besides, on CMNIST-sp, only GALA and Disc have some improvement over ERM.

limitations.value: The authors didn't discuss the limitations of the proposed method.

summary.value: The paper proposes a new framework called Graph invAriant Learning Assistant (GALA) to address the problem of learning invariance among data from different environments for out-of-distribution generalization on graphs. The authors argue that the performance of graph neural networks (GNNs) can be seriously degraded by graph distribution shifts caused by mismatches between the training and test graph distributions. title.value: Does Invariant Graph Learning via Environment Augmentation Learn Invariance?

TLDR.value: We found impossibility results of learning invariant graph representations without environment partitions, established the minimal assumptions for the feasibility of the problem and propose a novel solution.

abstract.value: Invariant graph representation learning aims to learn the invariance among data from different environments for out-of-distribution generalization on graphs. As the graph environment partitions are usually expensive to obtain, augmenting the environment information has become the de facto approach. However, the usefulness of the augmented environment information has never been verified. In this work, we find that it is fundamentally impossible to learn invariant graph representations via environment augmentation without additional assumptions. Therefore, we develop a set of minimal assumptions, including variation sufficiency and variation consistency, for feasible invariant graph learning. We then propose a new framework Graph invAriant Learning Assistant (GALA). GALA incorporates an assistant model that needs to be sensitive to graph environment changes or distribution shifts. The correctness of the proxy predictions by the assistant model hence can differentiate the variations in spurious subgraphs. We show that extracting the maximally invariant subgraph to the proxy predictions provably identifies the underlying invariant subgraph for successful OOD generalization under the established minimal assumptions. Extensive experiments on datasets including DrugOOD with various graph distribution shifts confirm the effectiveness of GALA.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return    

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=openreview.api.Note(
                id=submission.id
            ),
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
